name: Mississippi

gdl.nightCurfew: Intermediate drivers may not drive 10 p.m.-6 a.m. Sun.-Thu. and 11:30 p.m.-6 a.m. Fri.-Sat., unless accompanied by a licensed parent/guardian or for work

requiredDocuments: Proof of identity/lawful presence (original birth certificate or acceptable equivalent; no photocopies)
Social Security card or official document showing full SSN
Two proofs of Mississippi residency (e.g. utility bill, bank statement)
School Attendance Form if under 18 (dated within 30 days)
process.realIdNotes: A REAL ID requires a completed application, proof of identity/lawful presence, an SSN document, and two proofs of Mississippi residency; name-change documents are required when the current name differs from the birth record.
process.permitFee: $7 (regular Class R learner's permit, valid 2 years)
process.visionStandard: Vision exam required at issuance; specific acuity threshold not published on the referenced pages

facts.pointSuspensionThreshold: No point system; suspensions follow specific convictions rather than accumulated points
facts.moveOverRule: Move to a non-adjacent lane when safe, or slow down and proceed with caution, for stopped emergency and authorized vehicles with flashing lights
facts.schoolZoneSpeed: 15 mph when posted/flashing (varies by posted sign)

bacAdult.display: It is unlawful to drive with a blood/breath alcohol concentration of 0.08% or more (0.08 grams of alcohol per 100 mL of blood or per 210 L of breath) for a person above the legal drinking age.

conditions.detail: Applies to a person below the legal age to purchase alcohol; Mississippi sets an explicit 0.02% numeric 'zero tolerance' limit (not an any-detectable-amount rule).

bacUnder21.display: For drivers under the legal drinking age, Mississippi's zero-tolerance rule makes it unlawful to drive with a BAC of 0.02% or more.

conditions.detail: Applies to a person operating a commercial motor vehicle.

bacCommercial.display: A person operating a commercial motor vehicle may not drive with a BAC of 0.04% or more.

conditions.detail: Refusing the chemical test triggers a 90-day administrative license suspension (recorded here as 3 months) for a first occurrence with no prior DUI conviction/nonadjudication; it increases to 1 year for a person previously convicted or nonadjudicated under § 63-11-30. The suspension is a civil administrative sanction, not a separate crime.

impliedConsentRefusal.display: Under Mississippi's implied-consent law, refusing a breath/blood/urine test results in a 90-day administrative driver's-license suspension for a first occurrence (1 year if previously convicted/nonadjudicated for DUI); the refusal itself is not a separate criminal offense.

conditions.detail: Mississippi has no statewide statute prohibiting a driver or passenger from possessing or consuming an open alcoholic beverage in a moving vehicle (only driving while impaired/over the BAC limit is barred under § 63-11-30); Mississippi is not in compliance with the federal open-container standard of 23 U.S.C. § 154. Some municipalities/counties impose their own local open-container ordinances.

openContainerProhibited.display: Mississippi does not have a general statewide open-container law: it is not itself illegal for a driver or passenger to have or drink from an open container in a moving vehicle, though driving over the BAC limit or while impaired remains illegal, and local ordinances may prohibit open containers.

citation.label: Miss. Code Ann. § 63-11-30
citation.citation: Miss. Code Ann. § 63-11-30 (DUI is the only statewide alcohol-and-driving prohibition; no separate open-container statute)

conditions.detail: Suspension of regular driving privileges for a first DUI is governed by the § 63-11-23 framework (a 90-day suspension); a first offender may instead qualify for an interlock-restricted license under § 63-11-31 for the applicable period.

duiFirstSuspensionDays.display: A first DUI offense carries a 90-day driver's-license suspension under Mississippi's implied-consent/administrative framework; a first offender may alternatively obtain an ignition-interlock-restricted license.

conditions.detail: The statewide default maximum is 65 mph; the Mississippi Transportation Commission may raise the limit up to 70 mph on the Interstate Highway System and on controlled-access highways with four or more lanes, effective where posted.

ruralInterstateMaxMph.display: Mississippi's default statewide maximum is 65 mph, but the Transportation Commission may post up to 70 mph on interstates and four-or-more-lane controlled-access highways.

conditions.detail: Mississippi's speed statute sets no separate 'urban interstate' limit; the same 70 mph interstate ceiling applies where posted, and MDOT may post lower limits on individual (including urban) segments after an engineering study.

urbanInterstateMaxMph.display: Mississippi does not set a distinct urban-interstate speed limit; the 70 mph interstate ceiling applies where posted, with MDOT authorized to post lower limits on specific urban segments.

state.reason: Mississippi's speed statutes do not define a residential-district default speed. A single statewide default of 65 mph applies absent other posting (§ 63-3-501), and local authorities (counties/municipalities) may lower the limit on their streets and roads by ordinance after an engineering study, but no such local limit may be set below 15 mph (§ 63-3-511). There is no statutory residential-district figure comparable to states that set a 25/30 mph default.

residentialDefaultMph.display: Not applicable: Mississippi has no statutory residential-district default speed; the statewide default (65 mph) applies absent posting, and local authorities set lower residential limits by ordinance (never below 15 mph).

conditions.detail: Mississippi sets no single statewide school-zone speed number: county boards and municipal governing authorities set school-zone limits by order/resolution (based on an engineering study) that take effect when posted and may apply only during specified times (§ 63-3-515). The 15 mph value used here is the statutory floor for any local speed limit (§ 63-3-511) and the commonly posted school-zone figure; actual posted limits vary by location.

schoolZoneMph.display: School-zone speed limits in Mississippi are set locally by county/municipal authorities and posted (often 15 mph, which is the statutory minimum for any local limit); no single statewide school-zone number is fixed by statute.

conditions.detail: Mississippi expresses its basic-speed rule as a duty to decrease speed when approaching/crossing intersections, curves, or hill crests, on narrow/winding roadways, or when a special hazard exists as to pedestrians or other traffic — rather than a single 'reasonable and prudent' clause.

basicSpeedLaw.display: Mississippi requires a driver to reduce speed when conditions or hazards warrant (intersections, curves, hill crests, narrow/winding roads, or pedestrian/traffic hazards), regardless of the posted maximum.

rightTurnOnRed.display: After stopping, a driver facing a steady red signal may cautiously turn right unless a posted 'No Turn On Red' sign prohibits it, yielding to pedestrians and other traffic.

leftTurnOnRedFromOneWay.display: At the intersection of two one-way streets, a driver facing a steady red signal may cautiously turn left in the direction of one-way traffic after stopping, unless a posted 'No Turn On Red' sign prohibits it.

conditions.detail: Every operator and passenger of a passenger motor vehicle (one designed to carry 15 or fewer people) must wear a properly fastened safety belt while the vehicle is in forward motion; the chapter contains no secondary-enforcement limitation, so officers may stop and cite solely for a belt violation. Only the operator is fined ($25 aggregate) and the violation is not entered on the driving record.

seatBeltEnforcement.display: Mississippi requires all occupants of a passenger vehicle to buckle up and enforces the belt law as a primary offense (an officer may stop a vehicle solely for a seat-belt violation); the $25 fine falls on the driver and is not recorded on the driving record.

conditions.detail: Mississippi bans texting and accessing/posting to social-networking sites on a hand-held phone while driving (§ 63-33-1), but does NOT generally prohibit holding a phone to make or take a voice call; there is no broad handheld-device ban for adult drivers.

handheldPhone.display: Mississippi has no general handheld-phone ban — talking on a hand-held phone is not prohibited statewide — although writing/reading texts and using social media on a handheld device while driving is illegal.

texting.display: Any operator of a moving motor vehicle is prohibited from writing, sending, or reading a text message and from accessing, reading, or posting to a social-networking site using a hand-held mobile phone (a $100 civil penalty); the ban applies to all drivers.

moveOver.display: Approaching a stationary emergency vehicle, recovery/tow vehicle, utility-service vehicle, sanitation vehicle, or highway-maintenance vehicle displaying flashing lights, a driver must move into a non-adjacent lane when on a road with two or more lanes in that direction (if safe), or otherwise slow down and be prepared to stop; no fixed reduced mph is specified.

conditions.detail: Mississippi's statute does not use a 'wipers in use' trigger or a minutes-after-sunset offset. It requires lighted lamps during the period from sunset to sunrise, and at any other time when there is not enough light to render a person clearly discernible at 500 feet ahead. whenWipersOn=false and minutesAfterSunset=0 (lights required starting at sunset) are the closest schema-compatible approximation of that rule; see display for the exact standard.

headlightsRequired.display: Mississippi requires lighted front and rear lamps from sunset to sunrise, and at any other time when there is insufficient light to clearly see a person 500 feet ahead — a sunset-to-sunrise plus visibility standard, not a wipers-in-use or fixed sunset-offset rule.

parkFtFromHydrant.display: No vehicle may stop, stand, or park within 10 feet of a fire hydrant.

parkFtFromCrosswalk.display: No vehicle may stop, stand, or park within 20 feet of a crosswalk at an intersection.

parkFtFromStopSign.display: No vehicle may stop, stand, or park within 30 feet upon the approach to any flashing beacon, stop sign, or traffic-control signal located at the side of a roadway.

parkFtFromRailroad.display: No vehicle may stop, stand, or park within 15 feet of the nearest rail of a railroad crossing.

conditions.detail: Mississippi does not use a numeric driver's-license demerit-point system. License suspensions and revocations are tied to specific convictions (e.g., DUI under § 63-11-30) and statutory grounds, not to accumulated points.

pointSystem.display: Mississippi does not operate a driver's-license point (demerit) system; license actions are based on specific convictions rather than accumulated points.

citation.label: MS DPS Driver Service Bureau
citation.citation: Mississippi Department of Public Safety, Driver Service Bureau (no demerit-point system; suspensions follow specific convictions)

state.reason: Mississippi has no numeric point system, so there is no points-in-a-window threshold that triggers suspension. License suspensions/revocations instead follow specific convictions and statutory grounds (e.g., DUI under § 63-11-30, refusal under § 63-11-23).

pointSuspension.display: Not applicable: Mississippi does not assess points, so no point total triggers suspension; suspensions follow specific convictions instead.

citation.label: MS DPS Driver Service Bureau
citation.citation: Mississippi Department of Public Safety, Driver Service Bureau (conviction-based suspensions; no point threshold)

permitMinAgeMonths.display: A learner's permit may be issued to an applicant who is at least 15 years old (180 months).

conditions.detail: Applies to applicants under 18: a driver's license may be issued to a person at least 16 who has held a learner's permit for at least one (1) year without a DUI or moving-violation conviction; any such conviction restarts the one-year requirement.

permitHoldingMonths.display: An applicant under 18 must hold a learner's permit for at least 12 months (without a DUI or moving-violation conviction) before qualifying for a driver's license at age 16 or older.

state.reason: Mississippi's graduated-licensing statutes (§§ 63-1-9, 63-1-21) do not mandate a specific number of supervised behind-the-wheel practice hours as a condition of licensure; the learner's-permit holding period and supervision-while-driving requirements are set instead.

supervisedHoursTotal.display: Not applicable: Mississippi statute does not require a set number of supervised practice-driving hours for licensure.

state.reason: Because Mississippi does not require a total number of supervised practice hours (§§ 63-1-9, 63-1-21), there is likewise no statutory nighttime-hours subset.

supervisedHoursNight.display: Not applicable: Mississippi statute sets no required supervised nighttime practice-driving hours.

conditions.detail: Sunday through Thursday: an under-18 regular (intermediate) license holder may drive unsupervised only 6:00 a.m.-10:00 p.m.; unsupervised driving is therefore restricted from 10:00 p.m. (start 22) to 6:00 a.m. (end 6).

Friday and Saturday: the statute sets an 11:30 p.m. (23:30) start for the restriction; rounded here to 24 for schema compatibility (startHour24 is an integer) — see display for the exact 11:30 p.m. time. Restriction ends 6:00 a.m. (end 6). Exceptions apply for travel directly to/from work or an educational or extracurricular activity, and the supervision requirement applies during the first six months as a regular license holder.

gdlNightCurfew.display: An under-18 regular (intermediate) license holder may drive unsupervised only 6:00 a.m.-10:00 p.m. Sunday-Thursday and 6:00 a.m.-11:30 p.m. Friday-Saturday during the first six months of holding the license; outside those hours a licensed parent/guardian or other person 21+ must occupy the front seat, except when driving directly to/from work, school, or an extracurricular activity.

state.reason: Mississippi's graduated-licensing law (§ 63-1-21) imposes a nighttime supervision requirement on under-18 regular (intermediate) license holders but does not cap the number of passengers or restrict young-passenger occupancy for novice/young drivers, so there is no phase-1 passenger limit.

gdlPassengerPhase1.display: Not applicable: Mississippi does not impose a passenger-number limit on young/novice drivers during any graduated-licensing phase.

minLiability.display: Mississippi's minimum motor-vehicle liability limits are $25,000 for bodily injury/death of one person, $50,000 for bodily injury/death of two or more persons in one accident, and $25,000 for property damage.

crashReportThresholdUsd.display: A driver involved in a crash that causes injury or death, or total apparent property damage of $500 or more, must immediately notify law enforcement (local police within a municipality, otherwise the nearest sheriff's office or highway patrol station).
